title: Energy and Diet
content:
# Energy and Diet

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Explain how energy from food is measured
- Calculate energy requirements and content
- Understand the relationship between diet, energy, and body mass
- Interpret food labels and nutritional information

## Introduction

The **energy content** of food is essential for understanding diet and nutrition. Energy from food powers all body processes. Understanding energy values, requirements, and balance helps maintain a healthy body weight and overall health.

## Key Concepts

### Measuring Energy

**Units of energy:**

| Unit | Abbreviation | Conversion |
|------|-------------|------------|
| Joule | J | Base unit |
| Kilojoule | kJ | 1 kJ = 1000 J |
| Calorie | cal | 1 cal = 4.18 J |
| Kilocalorie | kcal | 1 kcal = 4.18 kJ |

**Note:** Food "calories" usually mean kilocalories (kcal).

### Energy Content of Nutrients

| Nutrient | Energy (kJ/g) | Energy (kcal/g) |
|----------|--------------|----------------|
| Carbohydrates | 17 | 4 |
| Proteins | 17 | 4 |
| Lipids (fats) | 39 | 9 |
| Alcohol | 29 | 7 |

**Key point:** Lipids provide more than twice the energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins.

### Calculating Energy in Food

**From mass of nutrients:**

$$\text{Energy} = (\text{mass of carbs} \times 17) + (\text{mass of protein} \times 17) + (\text{mass of fat} \times 39)$$

**Example:**
A food contains 30g carbohydrate, 10g protein, and 5g fat.

Energy = (30 × 17) + (10 × 17) + (5 × 39)
       = 510 + 170 + 195
       = 875 kJ

### Measuring Energy in Food (Experimental)

**Calorimetry:**

1. Weigh food sample
2. Burn food sample
3. Heat known mass of water
4. Measure temperature rise
5. Calculate energy released

**Calculation:**
$$\text{Energy (J)} = \text{mass of water (g)} \times 4.2 \times \text{temperature rise (°C)}$$

**Limitations:**
- Not all energy transferred to water
- Some heat lost to surroundings
- Incomplete combustion
- Results usually underestimated

### Daily Energy Requirements

**Factors affecting energy needs:**

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) | Energy at rest |
| Physical activity | More activity = more energy |
| Age | Growth increases needs |
| Sex | Males typically need more |
| Body size | Larger bodies need more |
| Temperature | Cold increases needs |
| Health | Some conditions increase needs |

### Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

**BMR is:**
- Energy used at complete rest
- For basic body functions
- About 60-75% of daily energy use

**BMR used for:**
- Heart beating
- Breathing
- Brain function
- Maintaining body temperature
- Cell processes

**Approximate BMR:**
- Women: ~5,500 kJ/day
- Men: ~7,000 kJ/day

### Physical Activity Level (PAL)

**Multiplier for total energy needs:**

| Activity level | PAL factor |
|---------------|------------|
| Sedentary (office work) | 1.4-1.5 |
| Moderately active | 1.6-1.7 |
| Very active | 1.8-2.0 |
| Extremely active (athletes) | 2.0-2.4 |

**Total energy = BMR × PAL**

### Energy Balance

**For weight maintenance:**
$$\text{Energy in} = \text{Energy out}$$

**For weight loss:**
$$\text{Energy in} < \text{Energy out}$$

**For weight gain:**
$$\text{Energy in} > \text{Energy out}$$

**Approximate values:**
- To lose 0.5 kg/week: reduce by ~3,500 kcal/week (500/day)
- 1 kg body fat ≈ 32,000 kJ of stored energy

### Reading Food Labels

**Typical information per 100g and per serving:**

| Nutrient | Amount |
|----------|--------|
| Energy | kJ and kcal |
| Fat (of which saturates) | grams |
| Carbohydrate (of which sugars) | grams |
| Fibre | grams |
| Protein | grams |
| Salt | grams |

**Traffic light labelling:**
- Green = low (healthy)
- Amber = medium (OK in moderation)
- Red = high (limit intake)

[DIAGRAM: Example food label with annotations]

### Recommended Daily Amounts

**Guideline Daily Amounts (GDA):**

| Nutrient | Women | Men |
|----------|-------|-----|
| Energy | 8,400 kJ (2,000 kcal) | 10,500 kJ (2,500 kcal) |
| Fat | 70g | 95g |
| Saturated fat | 20g | 30g |
| Carbohydrate | 260g | 300g |
| Sugars | 90g | 120g |
| Protein | 50g | 55g |
| Salt | 6g | 6g |
| Fibre | 30g | 30g |

### Energy Density

**Energy density** = energy per gram of food

| Food type | Energy density | Examples |
|-----------|---------------|----------|
| Low | < 4 kJ/g | Vegetables, fruits |
| Medium | 4-9 kJ/g | Lean meat, bread |
| High | > 9 kJ/g | Cheese, nuts, chocolate |

**Low energy density foods:**
- Fill you up with fewer calories
- Help with weight management
- Usually high in water and fibre

### Practical Applications

**Weight management strategies:**

| Strategy | How it works |
|----------|-------------|
| Reduce portion sizes | Less energy in |
| Choose low energy density foods | Feel full with less energy |
| Increase physical activity | More energy out |
| Reduce fat intake | Fat has most energy per gram |
| Reduce sugary drinks | Easy source of excess energy |

### Calculating Energy Expenditure

**Approximate energy use for activities:**

| Activity | Energy (kJ/min) |
|----------|----------------|
| Sleeping | 4 |
| Sitting | 6 |
| Walking | 15 |
| Running | 40 |
| Swimming | 25 |
| Cycling | 20 |

**Example calculation:**
30 minutes of running = 30 × 40 = 1200 kJ

## Common Exam Questions

- Calculate energy content from nutrient data
- Explain why different people have different energy needs
- Interpret food label information
- Explain energy balance and weight change

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** All calories are equal for health
- **Reality:** Energy is equal, but nutritional value varies

- **Misconception:** Eating fat makes you fat
- **Reality:** Excess energy from any source causes weight gain

- **Misconception:** Exercising means you can eat anything
- **Reality:** Exercise uses less energy than many think

- **Misconception:** Low-fat foods are always healthy
- **Reality:** They often have added sugar to compensate

## Practice Questions

1. State the energy value of 1 gram of carbohydrate. (1 mark)

2. A food contains 40g carbohydrate, 15g protein, and 10g fat. Calculate the total energy content in kJ. (3 marks)

3. Explain why a manual worker needs more energy than an office worker of the same age and sex. (2 marks)

4. A calorimetry experiment found that burning a food sample raised the temperature of 50g of water by 30°C. Calculate the energy released. (2 marks)

5. Explain what happens to body mass when energy intake exceeds energy expenditure over time. (3 marks)

6. Use the food label shown to calculate the percentage of daily energy requirement provided by one serving. (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Kilojoule (kJ) | Unit of energy (1000 joules) |
| Kilocalorie (kcal) | Unit of energy (4.18 kJ) |
| Basal metabolic rate | Energy used at rest for basic functions |
| Energy balance | Relationship between energy in and out |
| Energy density | Energy per gram of food |
| Calorimetry | Measuring energy by heat produced |
| GDA | Guideline Daily Amount |

## Summary

- Energy measured in kJ or kcal (1 kcal = 4.18 kJ)
- Carbohydrates: 17 kJ/g, Proteins: 17 kJ/g, Fats: 39 kJ/g
- Energy needs depend on BMR, activity, age, sex, and size
- Energy balance: in = out maintains weight
- Calorimetry measures energy by burning food and measuring heat
- Food labels provide energy and nutrient information
- Understanding energy helps manage weight and health
